excerpt: Cost per lead is easy to compare and mostly useless. Cost per booked appointment is more honest — with one important adjustment for seasonal trades.
meta_description: Why cost per booked appointment beats cost per lead when comparing channels, and how to adjust the calculation for seasonal trades.
author: SIT™ Editorial
seo_title: Cost Per Booked Appointment for Contractors — SIT™
title: Cost Per Booked Appointment — The Number Worth Comparing Across Channels
content:
### **Why Cost Per Lead Misleads** 

Cost per lead treats every lead as equivalent. A homeowner who filled out a form at midnight and a homeowner who agreed to a Tuesday appointment are counted the same way. They are not the same thing.  A channel producing cheap leads that rarely convert can look far better on paper than a channel producing fewer, better ones. 

### **The Calculation** 

Take everything spent on a channel over a period. Divide it by the number of appointments that were actually scheduled from it. That number — cost per booked appointment — is comparable across channels in a way cost per lead is not. 

### **What It Reveals** 

Most companies that run this calculation find their channel ranking changes. The cheapest source of leads is frequently not the cheapest source of appointments, sometimes by a wide margin. 

### **The Seasonal Adjustment That Matters** 

There is one situation where this calculation misleads badly, and it is common enough to be worth stating clearly.  In seasonal trades, outreach conducted outside the buying season produces relatively few immediate appointments and a large number of homeowners asking to be contacted at a specific later date. Judged on booked appointments alone, that work looks weak. It is not — it is a booked pipeline for the following season, and treating it as a failure is one of the more expensive mistakes a company can make.  The adjustment is straightforward: count scheduled appointments and dated follow-up requests separately, and judge off-season activity primarily on the second number. 

### **The Other Number Worth Pairing** 

What percentage of leads from each channel were contacted at all, and how quickly. Channels are often judged on conversion when the real variable was follow-up speed on the client side. 

### **Why We Recommend This Standard** 

We would rather be measured on cost per booked appointment than on lead volume. It is a harder standard and a more honest one — provided the seasonal adjustment above is applied, since otherwise it penalizes exactly the off-season work that builds the following year.
